name: Intuitive eating

lead: Intuitive eating, created by dietitians Evelyn Tribole and Elyse Resch, replaces diet rules with attention to hunger, fullness and satisfaction. It is discussed in eating disorder recovery and body image circles.
Reviews link it with better psychological outcomes; evidence on long-term weight and physical health is limited.

paras: Ten principles include rejecting diet mentality, honouring hunger and fullness, making peace with food and coping with emotions without food.
Critics note limited long-term weight data and that some medical conditions need structured diets. Lack of concrete rules can make it hard to apply.

lead: Intuitive eating is an approach to eating that centres on the body's hunger and satisfaction cues rather than external diet rules, aiming to build a positive relationship with food instead of weight control [1]. It was coined by registered dietitians Evelyn Tribole and Elyse Resch, whose book Intuitive Eating was first published in 1995 [2].

Its ten principles include rejecting the diet mentality, honouring hunger and fullness, making peace with food and coping with emotions without food [1][2]. Research links it with better psychological outcomes, while evidence on weight and physical health is mixed or limited [3][4][5].
infobox: Evelyn Tribole and Elyse Resch (registered dietitians)

paras: The framework rejects chronic dieting and moral labelling of foods, and emphasises permission to eat, attention to hunger and satiety, satisfaction, respecting the body and gentle movement [1][2]. It is not designed as a weight-loss method [1].

Tribole and Resch developed the approach from clinical work with chronic dieters in the early 1990s, and their book appeared in 1995 with later editions in 2000, 2012 and 2020, according to Grokipedia (an AI-generated source) [2]. Wikipedia notes the term first appeared in a 1990s peer-reviewed article [1]. Tylka published the Intuitive Eating Scale in 2006 and the revised IES-2 in 2013 [6].

A six-month randomised trial of 78 obese female chronic dieters compared a health-at-every-size programme that included intuitive eating with dieting and followed participants for two years [7]. A 2021 meta-analysis examined psychological correlates of intuitive eating [3], and reviews of health indicators and of interventions promoting eating by internal cues were published in 2014 [4][8]. A 2017 structured review covered mindfulness, mindful eating and intuitive eating [5]. Wikipedia summarises findings as associations with higher self-esteem and body appreciation, possible improvement in cholesterol, glucose and blood pressure, and limited evidence on long-term weight [1].

Researchers cited by Wikipedia say evidence on long-term weight outcomes is insufficient, that results vary between people, that some medical conditions may require prescribed diets, and that the lack of concrete food rules can make it hard to apply; Wikipedia also categorises the topic under pseudoscience, reflecting disputes about its evidence [1]. Observational links with lower BMI may reflect reverse causation [1].
The approach is discussed in eating disorder recovery and body image communities. Wikipedia says it may reduce eating disorder symptoms but that evidence is still developing [1].
